questions.clue: A rule that converts a sample into a value for an unknown population quantity.
questions.explanation: An estimator is the rule applied to the sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimator

questions.clue: The specific numerical result obtained after applying a rule to the observed data.
questions.explanation: An estimate is the result of applying an estimator to one sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimate

questions.clue: A range calculated from sample data by a method with a stated long-run success rate for containing the target parameter.
questions.explanation: The confidence rate describes the repeated-sampling behavior of the interval procedure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue: The stated long-run capture rate of an interval procedure under its model assumptions.
questions.explanation: For a valid 95% procedure, about 95% of repeated intervals capture the fixed target.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04

questions.clue: The reference claim evaluated by a significance test, often expressing no difference.
questions.explanation: The test assesses how unusual the evidence is under this reference claim.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 307, Null hypothesis

questions.clue: The claim that specifies how the population could differ from the test’s reference claim.
questions.explanation: The alternative determines which directions or values count against the null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Alternative hypothesis

questions.clue: Researchers record patients’ existing diets and follow their health without choosing diets for them.
questions.explanation: The researchers observe existing exposures without assigning them.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 308, Observational study

questions.clue: A coin toss determines which treatment each participant receives.
questions.explanation: Chance assigns treatment to enrolled participants.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 354, Random allocation

questions.clue: People receive a pill but are kept unaware of whether it contains the study drug.
questions.explanation: Hiding treatment identity from participants limits expectation effects.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 57, Blinding

questions.clue: A comparison pill looks just like the study drug but contains none of its active ingredient.
questions.explanation: A placebo mimics treatment without including its active component.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Placebo

questions.clue: One survey measures employment and current health during the same interview, with no follow-up.
questions.explanation: Exposure and outcome information are measured at one time in a cross-sectional study.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 116, Cross-sectional study

questions.clue: Researchers group people by a recorded exposure and follow both groups for new cases of illness.
questions.explanation: A cohort study follows a defined group to observe outcomes over time.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 90, Cohort study

questions.clue:
c × SE
where a symmetric interval is estimate ± c × SE
questions.explanation: In a symmetric interval, the multiplier times the standard error is the half-width.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04

questions.clue:
x̄ − c × SE
for a symmetric interval with c > 0
questions.explanation: Subtracting the margin of error gives the lower endpoint.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04

questions.clue:
x̄ + c × SE
for a symmetric interval with c > 0
questions.explanation: Adding the margin of error gives the upper endpoint.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04

questions.clue:
s / √n
for the mean of n independent observations with sample SD s
questions.explanation: Replacing the population standard deviation with s estimates the standard error of the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue:
2c × SE
for a symmetric interval x̄ ± c × SE
questions.explanation: The upper and lower limits each lie one margin of error from the center, so the total width is twice the margin.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 4, §§4.2–4.2.1, Confidence Intervals: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04

questions.clue:
P(reject H₀ given H₀ is true)
for a simple null hypothesis
questions.explanation: This is the probability of making a Type I error, rejecting a true null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type I error

questions.clue: The difference between an estimator’s average over repeated samples and its target parameter.
questions.explanation: Bias measures systematic departure in the estimator’s long-run average.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 45, Bias

questions.clue: An estimator becomes arbitrarily close to its target with probability approaching one as sample size grows.
questions.explanation: Consistency describes accuracy in probability as the sample grows.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 100, Consistency

questions.clue: A comparison of how much two unbiased estimators of the same parameter vary over repeated samples.
questions.explanation: Among unbiased estimators for one target, the smaller-variance estimator is more efficient.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 149, Efficiency

questions.clue: Under the null model, the chance of a test result at least as extreme as the observed result.
questions.explanation: Extremeness is measured by the chosen test in the direction or directions specified by its alternative.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 346, P-value

questions.clue: At a specified alternative, the long-run probability of rejecting the null hypothesis.
questions.explanation: Power is the probability of detecting the specified departure from the null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power

questions.clue: The set of test statistic values that trigger rejection of the reference claim.
questions.explanation: The decision rule rejects the null if the statistic lands in this set.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 115, Critical region

questions.clue: Researchers start with people with and without a disease, then compare past exposure between the two groups.
questions.explanation: Selection starts with disease status, and the study compares earlier exposures.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 69, Case-control study

questions.clue: Each participant receives both treatments in different periods, with treatment order assigned by chance.
questions.explanation: Each person receives more than one treatment in different periods.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 116, Crossover design

questions.clue: Researchers match one treated patient with one untreated patient of similar age, then compare within each pair.
questions.explanation: Pairing links comparable observations for a within-pair comparison.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 271, Matched pairs

questions.clue: Plots are grouped by soil type, then treatments are randomly assigned within each soil group.
questions.explanation: Blocking builds known plot differences into the design before treatment is assigned.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 58, Blocking

questions.clue: A trial assigns every combination of two temperatures and three processing speeds.
questions.explanation: A factorial experiment combines levels of two or more factors to study their effects.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 161, Factorial designs

questions.clue: Neither study participants nor the people who measure their outcomes are told which treatment was assigned.
questions.explanation: Both specified groups are kept unaware of treatment identity.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 142, Double-blind
questions.convention: Names the two masked groups because practices vary between trials.

questions.clue: The treatment group is younger, and age itself affects the outcome. What threatens a causal interpretation?
questions.explanation: Age is associated with treatment and also affects outcome, so the treatment comparison mixes the effects.
questions.reference: UC Berkeley STAT 2, Fall 2024, Module 1, Data collection and variables: https://stat2.berkeley.edu/fall-2024/

questions.clue: Researchers test for a decrease in wait time. An increase provides no evidence for their specified alternative.
questions.explanation: This test’s alternative specifies just one direction of departure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 311, One-sided test

questions.clue:
E[(θ̂ − θ)²]
where θ̂ estimates the fixed target θ
questions.explanation: The mean squared error averages the squared difference between estimator and target.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean squared error

questions.clue:
Set x̄ = Eθ[X] and solve for θ.
Assume one unknown parameter.
questions.explanation: The method equates a sample moment to the corresponding population moment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 277, Method of moments

questions.clue:
The value of θ that maximizes L(θ)
for the observed data.
questions.explanation: The maximizing parameter value is the maximum likelihood estimate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 273, Maximum likelihood estimation

questions.clue:
(x̄ − μ₀) / (s / √n)
for a hypothesized mean μ₀ and sample SD s
questions.explanation: The one-sample t statistic uses an estimated standard error for a single sample mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Student’s t-distribution

questions.clue: P(do not reject H₀ given a specified alternative is true)
questions.explanation: This is the probability of making a Type II error at the specified alternative.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type II error

questions.clue:
(x̄ − μ₀) / (σ / √n)
for known population SD σ and hypothesized mean μ₀
questions.explanation: The z statistic uses the known population standard deviation in its standard error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 468, z-test

questions.clue:
The number c satisfying P(Z > c) = α
when Z follows its null distribution.
questions.explanation: The critical value is the cutoff for the test statistic.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 115, Critical value

questions.clue: Keep all values θ₀ for which the matching two-sided test of H₀: θ = θ₀ does not reject at level α.
questions.explanation: Inverting a family of tests gives a confidence set from the null values not rejected.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 415, Lesson 10, confidence interval and hypothesis test duality: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat415/Lesson10

questions.clue: The population quantity a study is trying to estimate, before choosing an analysis rule.
questions.explanation: The estimand defines the target, such as a population mean difference.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 154, Estimand

questions.clue: A rule whose expected value exactly equals the target parameter at every parameter value in the model.
questions.explanation: Across repeated samples at a fixed parameter, the average result equals that parameter.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 440, Unbiased

questions.clue: A summary that retains all the sample’s information about the parameter under the specified model.
questions.explanation: Given this statistic, the conditional distribution of the data contains no further dependence on the parameter.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 420, Sufficient statistic

questions.clue: Estimate an unknown function of a parameter by substituting a sample estimate for that parameter.
questions.explanation: The unknown parameter is replaced by its estimate inside the function.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Plug-in principle

questions.clue: Each volunteer stays on the one treatment they were assigned for the full follow-up.
questions.explanation: Separate treatment groups are followed at the same time.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 316, Parallel groups design

questions.clue: A clinic describes six patients with an unusual condition, without a separate comparison group.
questions.explanation: A case series describes multiple cases without a comparator group.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 70, Case series

questions.clue: Old employment files identify groups with different past exposures. Later disease records already exist for both groups.
questions.explanation: The groups are defined by exposure, and historical records provide outcomes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 370, Retrospective cohort study

questions.clue: A crossover trial leaves a treatment-free gap between periods so the first treatment can wear off.
questions.explanation: The gap reduces the chance that the previous treatment affects the next period.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 453, Wash-out period

questions.clue:
x̄ ± c × s/√n
where c comes from a t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: The t multiplier and sample standard deviation produce an interval for one population mean.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT Online, S.2 Confidence Intervals, t-interval and equal-tail multipliers: https://online.stat.psu.edu/statprogram/reviews/statistical-concepts/confidence-intervals

questions.clue:
x̄ ± c × σ/√n
where σ is known and c is a standard normal cutoff
questions.explanation: With known population standard deviation, a normal cutoff sets the confidence interval’s margin.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 415, Lesson 6, Theorem 6.1, Z-Interval for a Mean: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat415/Lesson06

questions.concept: estimated standard error of a proportion
questions.clue:
√[p̂(1 − p̂) / n]
for an observed proportion p̂ and n independent trials
choices: Estimated standard error of a proportion
Standard error under a specified null
questions.answer: Estimated standard error of a proportion
questions.explanation: The sample proportion substitutes for the unknown population probability in the standard error.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 8, §8.1 Inference for One Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson08

questions.clue:
Σᵢ (xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)
for n > 1 independent draws with a common finite variance
questions.explanation: With the n − 1 correction, the estimator’s expectation equals the population variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance

questions.clue: A range designed to contain a new individual observation at a stated long-run rate.
questions.explanation: Predicting an individual includes variation of the new observation itself.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 462, §4.11 Prediction Interval for a New Response: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat462/node/127/

questions.clue: A range intended to contain at least a chosen fraction of the population with a stated confidence level.
questions.explanation: The target is a fraction of the population, such as at least 90% of individual values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 432, Tolerance interval

questions.clue: A significance test whose alternative allows a population mean to differ from its reference in either direction.
questions.explanation: Departures above and below the null value can provide evidence against the null.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 438, Two-sided test

questions.clue: A difference is large enough to matter in its real-world setting, even before considering its p-value.
questions.explanation: Practical relevance depends on the size and consequences of the effect.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 6, Hypothesis Testing Part 2, Practical Significance: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson06

questions.clue: The extent to which an estimator gives similar values across repeated samples.
questions.explanation: A smaller sampling standard deviation indicates greater precision.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 335, Precision

questions.clue: A quantitative measure of how large a group difference or association is.
questions.explanation: An effect size expresses magnitude, such as a mean difference in original or standardized units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 148, Effect size

questions.clue: A trial finds a treatment effect and rejects no effect, but in truth the treatments are equally effective.
questions.explanation: The test rejected a true null hypothesis.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type I error

questions.clue: A test fails to detect a real treatment effect and leaves the no-effect hypothesis unrejected.
questions.explanation: The test failed to reject a false null hypothesis.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 439, Type II error

questions.clue: A trial analyzes patients under their originally assigned groups, even when some switch treatments.
questions.explanation: Keeping original groups preserves the randomized comparison for the assignment strategy.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Intention-to-treat analysis

questions.clue: A recruiter confirms eligibility and enrolls a participant before a central service reveals the upcoming assignment.
questions.explanation: Concealing upcoming assignments prevents foreknowledge from influencing who is enrolled.
questions.reference: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, v5.1, Chapter 8, allocation concealment: https://training.cochrane.org/sites/training.cochrane.org/files/public/uploads/resources/Handbook5_1/Chapter_8_Handbook_5_2_8.pdf

questions.clue: Some volunteers report relief after an inert pill because they expected it to help.
questions.explanation: Expectations can affect outcomes even if the pill lacks an active ingredient.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 327, Placebo effect

questions.clue: One treatment is a pill and the other an injection. Each group receives its active treatment and the other route’s look-alike placebo.
questions.explanation: The paired delivery routes make treatment identity harder to infer.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 142, Double-dummy technique

questions.clue:
p₁ − p₂
where p₁ and p₂ are two groups’ event probabilities
questions.explanation: Subtracting the risks gives the absolute difference on the probability scale.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 3, Two-Way Tables and Relative Risk: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson03

questions.clue:
p₁ / p₂
where p₁ and p₂ are group risks and p₂ > 0
questions.explanation: Dividing the probabilities gives risk in group one relative to group two.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 3, Two-Way Tables and Relative Risk: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson03

questions.clue:
[p₁/(1 − p₁)] / [p₂/(1 − p₂)]
for group probabilities strictly between 0 and 1
questions.explanation: Convert each probability to odds, then divide the two odds.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Odds ratio

questions.clue:
α/2
for each of the two equally sized tails outside the central area 1 − α
questions.explanation: The two tails share the total probability α evenly.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT Online, S.2 Confidence Intervals, t-interval and equal-tail multipliers: https://online.stat.psu.edu/statprogram/reviews/statistical-concepts/confidence-intervals

questions.clue:
(x̄₁ − x̄₂) / √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)
for independent means and a null difference of zero
questions.explanation: Welch’s standard error uses the two separate sample variances.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 555, §2.6, t-tests, Welch’s two-sample t statistic: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat555/node/36/

questions.clue:
1 − β
where β is the probability of missing a fixed real effect
questions.explanation: The chance of detecting the fixed effect is one minus the chance of missing it.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 334, Power

questions.clue: The probability of making one or more false rejections across a family of tests.
questions.explanation: The event is at least one rejected true null in the entire family.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 164, Familywise error rate

questions.clue: A treatment administered earlier continues to influence outcomes during the next treatment period.
questions.explanation: Residual effects from the earlier treatment contaminate the later period.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 69, Carryover effects

questions.clue: A trial comparison restricted to participants meeting predefined adherence requirements.
questions.explanation: Restriction by adherence can change the comparability initially provided by random assignment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 324, Per protocol

questions.clue: An estimate is recalculated repeatedly, leaving out a different single observation each time.
questions.explanation: Leave-one-out estimates can be combined to assess bias or standard error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 226, Jackknife

questions.clue: Under an exchangeable no-group-effect model, shuffle group labels many times and compare the observed mean difference with the shuffled differences.
questions.explanation: Shuffling labels builds a reference distribution under the null model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 324, Permutation test

questions.clue: For paired measurements with no ties, a researcher counts increases and compares the count with a fair-binomial reference.
questions.explanation: The sign test uses directions of change without their magnitudes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 393, Sign test

questions.clue: Participants know their treatments, but the reviewer scoring their scans sees anonymized IDs without group labels.
questions.explanation: Keeping assessors unaware can reduce differences in judgment across groups.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 57, Blinding

questions.clue: A factory needs an upper limit for its mean defect concentration at a chosen confidence level, with no lower endpoint.
questions.explanation: This procedure limits the parameter from above while allowing all smaller values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 99, Confidence interval

questions.clue:
(x₁ + x₂) / (n₁ + n₂)
for independent success counts x₁ and x₂ with a shared probability
questions.explanation: Add all successes and divide by the combined number of trials.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 9, Inference for Two Samples: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson09

questions.clue:
d̄ ± c × s_d/√n
where c is a t cutoff and d is the within-pair difference
questions.explanation: Use one observation per pair, namely its difference.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 500, Lesson 7, Comparing Two Population Parameters: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/Lesson07

questions.clue:
α/m
used as each local cutoff when testing m hypotheses to control familywise error
questions.explanation: The sum of the local Type I error bounds is at most α.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bonferroni correction

questions.clue:
(p̂ − p₀) / √[p₀(1 − p₀)/n]
for a sample proportion p̂ and hypothesized p₀
questions.explanation: The denominator uses the null probability p₀ in the standard error.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 8, §8.1 Inference for One Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson08

questions.clue: MSE of θ̂ = Var(θ̂) + [E(θ̂) − θ]²
questions.explanation: Expanding squared error shows variance and squared bias add to total mean squared error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean squared error

questions.clue:
√[p̂₁(1 − p̂₁)/n₁ + p̂₂(1 − p̂₂)/n₂]
for two independent sample proportions
questions.explanation: Estimate each group’s variance separately when constructing the usual interval for their difference.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 200, Lesson 9, Inference for Two Samples: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson09
